title: Towards powerful oracy for all.
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington welcomes the new wave of enthusiasm for oracy in England while being exasperated by the arguments mounted against it, which he calls lazy, shallow or deliberately conflated. He lists the common ones, that oracy is a bolt-on, competes with writing, is generic and knowledge-free, caused Wales's PISA slide, or lowers standards, and answers each from his years as head of KEGS and from the Voice 21 framework. In his reading the cognitive and linguistic strands make oracy a vehicle for building knowledge, while the Voice 21 benchmarks such as values every voice and harnessing oracy to elevate learning give schools a way to gauge practice. He then names the pitfalls he shares with critics: reintroducing formal speaking and listening exams, which would let the summative tail wag the formative dog, and carving out dedicated oracy lessons that take time from other subjects. He ends optimistically, treating oracy as the next wave after cognitive science and offering a set of practical lesson-level questions teachers can ask.
points: Sherrington treats oracy as talk that does the work of learning, so its cognitive and linguistic strands are about engaging with curriculum knowledge rather than generic speaking skills.
He answers the standards objection from experience, arguing that at a high-attaining school with knowledge at the centre of the curriculum oracy was a driving force and raised the bar.

He shares two critics' worries, that a return to high-stakes speaking and listening exams would hold back oracy because of bias, inflation, unreliability and workload, and that separate oracy lessons would reinforce the idea that oracy is an extra.
He argues for daily classroom practice (Mode A) over formal debating and presentations (Mode B), where the action is in cold calling, think-pair-share and talk protocols.
He ends with five diagnostic questions tied to the Voice 21 strands and benchmarks, such as whether everyone is expected to think and whether every student gets to rehearse new vocabulary.
quotes: So, to me, talk is just a fundamental part of the whole business of teaching and learning. And this means talk for everyone.
The very weird idea that oracy is a bolt-on; a set of things you do outside of normal teaching rather than being central to it. Nobody has time for extras, obviously.

The oracy framework divides oracy into four strands. The cognitive strand is central to it – oracy is fundamentally about thinking and making sense of ideas in the curriculum. Oracy is all about engaging with knowledge.
Talk does not mean ‘they repeat back what I just said verbatim’. Talk means they engage in dialogue.

I don’t trust Lucy Powell, England’s current Education Secretary, to understand assessment well enough not to mess this up. To me it’s entirely consistent to advocate for deepening oracy across the curriculum and to say that we don’t need speaking and listening exams back.

But – please don’t suggest schools carve out time for oracy lessons such that this requires other subjects to lose time. We already don’t have enough time to cover the curriculum we have and all this does is reinforce that oracy is outside the curriculum; an extra; content-free.
In my view, there’s no going back from our work grappling with cognitive science and the importance of knowledge. Oracy builds on that; it’s the next wave.
Is everyone expecting to think? Cognitive strand. With oracy in mind, cold calling, for example, has moral purpose – why would you run a room so only some students think and get their ideas aired?
